extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in political communication, journalism studies, and media studies investigating press–state relations and international news sourcing
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative, cross‑national analysis of news agencies' source structures and issue framing during an international crisis using indexing theory and social network analysis. The method codes nationality and framing of sources, constructs two‑mode affiliation networks, and interprets centrality as salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing theory premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing theory is based on several premises: (a) The theory applies to elite press organizations (i.e., prestigious national newspapers and news‑wire services); (b) the theory mainly applies to legitimate and credible sources, excluding societal voices that involve civil disobedience, protests, or lawless acts; and (c) the theory best fits areas such as foreign affairs, military decisions, trade, and macroeconomic policy (Bennett, 1990).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indexing as a framework when studying elite press or wire services and legitimate/credible official sources in topics like foreign policy and security; be cautious applying it to grassroots/social movement coverage or non‑elite outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of the source structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The source structure outlines how sources are used in media coverage and reflects profound political or cultural causes. Components include types of sources (e.g., government officials, experts), the diversity of sources, and the tone of quotes (e.g., positive, negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing source structure, code for source type, measure diversity (variety of source types/nationalities), and capture tone of quotations. Expect heavy reliance on official sources in international/crisis coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality of news sources (coding categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nationality of news sources was coded as: the countries involved in the six‑party talks (the United States, China, South Korea, Japan, North Korea, Russia), global sources (any source apart from specific nationality, such as officials of the United Nations), and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify each quoted/source actor into one of these nationality buckets to assess press–state relations; 'global' captures transnational/unnationalized sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue framing categories (seven frames)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven categories concerning the impact of the missile crisis and conflict resolution were constructed: domestic policy, international policy, domestic security, international security, economy, internal situation of North Korea (North Korea domestic policy), and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish policy frames from security frames (doves vs hawks) and domestic vs international dimensions; economy is treated without domestic/international split; ‘others’ catches frames outside these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing policy vs security frames and domestic vs international context
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the frame of policy is distinguished from security: doves' perspectives (e.g., peace negotiations) = policy; hawks' perspectives (e.g., military affairs) = security. Second, frames carry domestic or international agenda dimensions depending on national interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code both the substantive frame (policy vs security) and whether it is oriented to domestic or international concerns; this helps link framing to national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article inclusion/exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: News articles irrelevant to the North Korean missile issue were excluded. Also exempted from the analysis were articles of fewer than 100 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling a dataset, filter by relevant keywords and remove very short items (<100 words) to ensure substantive content; document databases and search terms used (e.g., 'North Korea' and 'missile').

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and sampling procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles were collected by searching with the keywords 'North Korea' and 'missile' from multiple online news databases, including LexisNexis, Xinhua’s database, and Naver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent keyword queries across multiple databases and record source counts by stage; remove irrelevant returns manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis staging (temporal segmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study divided the crisis into three stages, each corresponding to one of three long‑range missile launches: Stage 1: July 5–October 8, 2006; Stage 2: April 5–May 24, 2009; Stage 3: December 12, 2012–February 11, 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment coverage into theoretically meaningful stages tied to events to examine dynamics over time; justify stage boundaries by external events (launches, tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: News agency selection rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Three news agencies were selected: Associated Press (AP) in the United States, Xinhua in China, and Yonhap in South Korea. News agencies provide unique locales for study as they function as major sources of international news and reflect country foreign policy and political stance. Their relation to the state varies (e.g., Xinhua and Yonhap subsidized by government; AP independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose agencies with contrasting state relationships/business models to examine press–state variation; document subsidy/ownership context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑mode (affiliated) network construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A two‑mode network (affiliated network) was constructed where rows are nationality of news sources and columns are issue framing by news sources; the affiliated relationship links nationalities to frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a nationality×frame matrix so country nodes and frame nodes are linked via co‑occurrence; use two‑mode analysis to derive relationships among countries (via shared frames) and among frames (via shared nationalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality metric: degree centrality and calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree centrality was used to represent the popularity of a certain actor in the network. Degree centrality is calculated by the number of ties each actor acquires. An individual actor's centrality score is obtained by dividing degree centrality by the sum of all actor centralities (Wasserman & Faust, 1994).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use degree centrality as a normalized salience measure; higher centrality = greater prominence/salience in source or framing networks. Report numerical centrality tables across stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting centrality as salience
rubrics_metrics.description: Centrality score represents the salience of nationality or issue framing: when a country‑of‑origin news source becomes more salient it gains a higher centrality score; salience can be determined by association with other sources (not just frequency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret centrality increases as greater prominence or brokerage power in discourse; complement frequency counts with network centrality to capture relational salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder reliability procedure and threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Data were coded by two graduate‑student coders fluent in English, Mandarin, and Korean. Ten percent of the total sample was coded to compare results, satisfying the threshold of intercoder reliability. The final intercoder reliability was above .77 (Scott’s pi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bilingual/multilingual coders for cross‑national media; double‑code a sample (e.g., 10%) and report reliability (Scott's pi or Cohen’s kappa) with a stated acceptable threshold (here > .77).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame coding special rules (economy and North Korea domestic policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy was added as a category given interdependence of world economy and international conflicts; the frame of economics was not given any domestic or international dimension. The domestic policy of North Korea was included because missile launches are often related to internal affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat economy as a standalone, non‑domestic/non‑international coded frame; explicitly code for NK domestic policy where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological limitation and descriptive nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytic benefit of social network analysis lies in assessing interrelated connections among nations and framing, but the results are descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that SNA provides descriptive maps of relationships and centralities; supplement with qualitative explication and be cautious about causal claims.
